titre: Kant (1795): Perpetual Peace Runs Through the Republic, Not Democracy
accroche: The democratic peace claims Kant as its source, yet he demands separation of powers, representation, and a federation, and judges democracy without representatives to be despotic.
contenu_vulgarise:
Kant is often presented as the father of the “democratic peace”: democracies do not go to war with one another, and he supposedly announced it in 1795. The text of *Perpetual Peace* is more demanding, and it does not quite say that.

## The Argument From the Wallet

The first definitive article of the treaty Kant imagines holds that the civil constitution of every state must be republican. His reasoning is a calculation of costs. If the consent of the subjects is required to decide on war, “nothing is more natural” than for them to weigh the matter before embarking on “such a bad business”: they will have to fight themselves, pay for the war out of their own property, repair the devastation, and carry a debt that new wars will prevent them from ever repaying. In a constitution that is not republican, by contrast, the head of state is not a citizen but the owner of the state: war costs him nothing, and he can decide on it for the “most trifling reasons,” like a pleasure outing. (Quotations follow Mary Campbell Smith's English translation.)

## “Republican” Is Not “Democratic”

For Kant, the word designates a form of government: legislative power is separated from executive power, and the representative system is the condition of any republican administration, without which it is “despotic and violent.” Democracy, in the sense of the people governing themselves, departs from this: under a democratic constitution, he writes, everyone wants to be the master, and republicanism can be reached only through a violent revolution. A monarchy or an aristocracy, on the other hand, can approach it by governing in the spirit of a representative system.

## One Condition Among Others

The republic is not enough. Kant adds a second article: the law of nations must be founded on a federation of free states, an alliance of a particular kind that he calls foedus pacificum, a “pact of peace,” which would differ from a pactum pacis, the ordinary peace treaty, in that the latter ends only one war, whereas the former would seek to end all wars forever. Wikipedia points out that Kant held the republican constitution to be only one of several necessary conditions.

## The Shift

The contemporary theory came later: Michael Doyle popularized it in 1983, speaking of “liberal” regimes (market economy, legal rights of citizens, representative government), a category in which he places the constitutional monarchy of Louis-Philippe. And it does not say that democracies are peaceful: only that they avoid war with one another. Between the 1795 text and the theory, the word “democracy” took the place of “republic,” a shift for which Kant is not responsible.

repere.texte: Kant writes: “nothing is more natural than that they should weigh the matter well, before undertaking such a bad business” (if the consent of the subjects is required to decide on war).
repere.source: Kant, Perpetual Peace (1795), definitive article 1, trans. M. Campbell Smith (1903), Internet Archive

carte.punch: Kant never wrote “democracies do not go to war with one another.”
carte.idee: In Perpetual Peace (1795), Kant demands a republican constitution: separation of powers and representation. A democracy without representatives strikes him as despotic. He adds a federation of free states.

quiz.question: Why, for Kant, does a republican constitution make war less likely?
choix: Citizens, who pay for war out of their own property, will not decide on it lightly if their consent is required
Republics are governed by elites who know and respect one another
Trade between republics makes wars economically pointless for their merchants
Democracy gives the people the wisdom to renounce armed conflict
quiz.explication: Kant reasons in terms of costs: those who pay for war will hesitate to decide on it. He invokes neither trade nor respect among elites, and he judges democracy without a representative system to be incompatible with republicanism.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What distinguishes the foedus pacificum from the pactum pacis, for Kant?
choix: The foedus pacificum seeks to end war forever, while the pactum pacis ends only one war
The foedus pacificum is a treaty between two states only, while the pactum pacis applies to federations
The pactum pacis requires a single world government, which the foedus pacificum does not
The foedus pacificum is signed only by monarchs, the pactum pacis by republics
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text distinguishes the two pacts: the pactum pacis, an ordinary treaty, ends only one war, whereas the foedus pacificum aims at a definitive peace, according to Kant.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why, according to Kant, does democracy without representatives lead to republicanism only through violence?
choix: Because citizens lack the education needed to legislate
Because democracy abolishes the private property of citizens
Because everyone wants to be the master, and only a violent revolution leads there
Because democracy always leads to a civil war between classes
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Kant writes that under a democratic constitution everyone wants to be the master, and that republicanism can be reached only through a violent revolution, not through education or civil war.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Michael Doyle do with Kant's theory in 1983?
choix: He showed that absolute monarchies are more peaceful than republics
He popularized the theory in 1983, speaking of “liberal” regimes, a category that included Louis-Philippe
He produced the first English translation of Kant's text
He renamed republics “democracies” in Kant's own writings
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Doyle popularizes the theory in 1983 under the name of liberal regimes, a category in which he places the constitutional monarchy of Louis-Philippe, without touching Kant's text.
